title: Apply quality principles in everyday cleaning tasks

lessons.title: What quality cleaning means
lessons.html:
Clean is part of the job

On a grain farm or at a silo, cleaning is not extra work. It is part of the work. Dirty floors, old grain in corners and dust on machines bring insects, rats and fires. Clients also check how clean we are. A clean site shows that we care about the grain.

What is quality?

Quality means doing the job right, the first time, every time. A quality clean is a clean that:

  • is done the way the work instruction says,
  • leaves no old grain, dust or spills behind,
  • is finished on time,
  • is safe for you and for others,
  • can be checked by your supervisor and passes.

Who is the customer?

Everybody who uses the place after you is your customer. The next shift is your customer. The truck driver who loads grain is your customer. The farmer who stores maize in the silo is a customer. If you leave a mess, they get the problem.

Why old grain is a problem

Old grain left in a bin, auger or under a conveyor is where weevils and other insects breed. When new grain comes in, the insects move into it. One handful of old, wet maize can spoil many tons of good maize. That is why we clean every corner, also the places that nobody sees.

Know your standard

Your supervisor will show you the cleaning standard for your area. It may be a checklist on the wall or a work instruction. Read it or ask someone to read it with you. If you do not understand a step, ask. It is better to ask than to do it wrong.

Remember: a clean that looks good from far away but has dirt in the corners is not a quality clean.

lessons.title: Doing the cleaning task step by step
lessons.html:
Plan before you clean

Before you start, stop and think. Look at the area. What must be cleaned? What tools do you need? Is anything dangerous?

Get ready

  1. Get your work instruction or checklist.
  2. Put on your personal protective equipment (PPE): dust mask, safety boots, gloves and, where needed, safety glasses and hearing protection.
  3. Collect your tools: brooms, brushes, scrapers, shovels, dust pans, bags or bins.
  4. Check that the tools are clean and not broken.

Safety first

  • Never clean inside an auger, conveyor, elevator or bin while the machine can start. The machine must be switched off and locked out by an authorised person.
  • Never go into a silo or bin alone. Grain can flow and bury a person in seconds.
  • Do not use compressed air to blow dust onto people or into the air near hot machines. Grain dust can burn and explode.
  • Do not mix cleaning chemicals. Use only what your supervisor gives you and read the label.

Clean from top to bottom

Start high and work down. Dust falls. If you sweep the floor first and then brush the beams, the floor gets dirty again. Then work from the back of the room to the door, so you do not walk over the clean floor.

Deal with the waste

Put swept grain, dust and rubbish in the right bin or bag. Spilled grain may go to a screenings bin; rubbish goes to the waste area. Never leave a pile of sweepings in a corner. Rats and insects will find it.

Put tools away

Clean your tools, check them and put them back in their place. Report a broken broom or shovel to your supervisor so it can be replaced.

lessons.title: Checking and improving your work
lessons.html:
Check your own work

When you finish, do not just walk away. Look at the area again, slowly. Use the checklist. Ask yourself:

  • Is there grain in the corners, under the conveyor or behind the doors?
  • Is there dust on beams, ledges and motor covers?
  • Are the walkways clear?
  • Is all the waste removed?
  • Are all tools packed away?

If you find something, fix it now. This is called checking your own work. It saves time because the supervisor does not have to send you back.

Report problems

Sometimes you find a problem you cannot fix. Tell your supervisor quickly. Examples:

  • a leaking roof that makes grain wet,
  • rat droppings or holes in the wall,
  • live insects in the grain,
  • a broken guard on a machine,
  • a cleaning chemical that is finished.

Your supervisor will write it down so that it can be fixed. Reporting is part of quality work.

Work as a team

Cleaning is often team work. Agree who cleans which part. Help a team member who is behind. When the shift changes, tell the next person what is done and what is still open.

Getting better

Quality is about getting better every day. If you see a faster or safer way to clean, tell your supervisor. Maybe a longer brush will reach the high beams. Maybe a bin closer to the work will save walking. Good ideas from workers make the whole farm better.

Key points

  • Quality cleaning means doing it right the first time, the way the standard says.
  • Old grain and dust bring insects, rats and fire risk.
  • Never clean inside a machine or bin unless it is switched off and locked out.
  • Clean from top to bottom and from the back to the door.
  • Check your own work and report problems you cannot fix.
